look_here_first: NATIVE BROAD-RANGE HAIRY WOODLAND BROME: unlike the other three installed annual Bromus species, this is a PERENNIAL with a persistent rooted crown, relatively broad soft blades, and a drooping open panicle in wooded/shady settings. Mature spikelets and comparatively shorter awns support the ID, but the existing 389×589 source photo only proves general habit: it cannot show the ligule or actual lemma hairs.

best_field_traits: Native perennial of shaded or moist woodland understory; intact old crown is essential to confirm perennial habit.
Relatively broad grass blades, frequently soft hairy closed sheaths, long arching leafy flowering culms.
Open drooping panicle, many-flowered spikelets frequently ~13–30 mm; the original low-res photo supports habit only.
Fertile lemma short straight awn often ~3–8 mm, not strongly long/curved like mature Japanese brome.
Nonnative rescuegrass can be annual, biennial or a short-lived perennial; habitat and perennial impression ALONE do not exclude it.
Rescuegrass spikelets are broadly flattened/keeled with nearly absent awns, not the typical narrower awned woodland brome.
what_to_photograph_for_confirmation: High-res whole plant with base showing perennial crown
Visible lower closed sheath and hairy node closeup
Glumes, lemmas, and whether mature upper internodes are hairy
crew_field_check: LOOK AT THE SPIKELET, NOT JUST THE DROOP: all four bromes have several florets stacked along one spikelet, often with lemma awns. First decide ANNUAL vs PERENNIAL, then count florets, measure the entire spikelet, individual lemma and awn, and inspect the glume veins and leaf sheath hairs. Nodding inflorescences or long awns alone are not a species ID.
Measure actual mature spikelet(s) with a millimeter ruler.
Inspect lemma/glume or true ligule ONLY where detailed pixels or a collected macro are actually available.
Record uncertain grass to genus, don't force the species from one photo.

comparisons.key_distinctions: WOODLAND: longer-lived tuft + broad soft leaves, drooping shaded understory panicle; rescuegrass can mimic perennial habit, so verify actual narrow vs broad compressed spikelet and awn placement before calling native.

field_matrix.where_to_look: Entire panicle BRANCHES + 2–3 mature awned spikelets, lower sheath, measure lemma and awn.
field_matrix.field_characters: Winter annual; thin arching/kinked drooping branches; spikelets often 15–25 mm with ~6–11 florets; divergent/bent awns ~8–13 mm.
field_matrix.difficult_overlap: Often overlaps native Texas brome in seedhead size and shape. Use glume veins and scaled lemma/awn measurements.
field_matrix.quick_rule: Kinked long-pediceled loose head + divergent awns favors Japanese; never declare invasive from size alone.

field_matrix.where_to_look: Mature WHOLE long spikelets and florets counted against a millimeter ruler.
field_matrix.field_characters: Annual with conspicuously long pointed many-flowered spikelets ~25–50 mm, often 8–20 florets; lemma 12–18 mm, awn 6–12 mm.
field_matrix.difficult_overlap: Large rescuegrass may have similarly long spikelets, but rescuegrass is VERY flattened and awns tiny or absent.
field_matrix.quick_rule: Long spear of overlapping florets with clear awns, not broad flattened oat-shaped head, raises lanceolate.

field_matrix.taxon: Texas brome · Bromus texensis (native Texas; county unaudited)
field_matrix.where_to_look: Mature lemma and true first/second glumes on one intact spikelet with 1-mm scale and backlight.
field_matrix.field_characters: Annual with slender open sometimes few-spikeleted panicle; lemma ~9–12 mm, awn ~6–10 mm, lower glume 1 vein, upper 3.
field_matrix.difficult_overlap: Japanese brome also annual with awned slender multi-flowered spikelets; yellow anthers and green hue not unique.
field_matrix.quick_rule: Glume vein count and measured awn/lemma are the decisive follow-up before native/invasive decision.

field_matrix.where_to_look: Turn one mature spikelet SIDEWAYS, inspect its flat keel and lemma awn length.
field_matrix.field_characters: Open or drooping panicle with relatively large strongly flattened broad, oatlike spikelets typically ~20–40 mm; one lemma awn usually absent or very SHORT, often 0–4 mm.
field_matrix.difficult_overlap: Lanceolate/woodland brome sometimes large too; rescuegrass has distinctly compressed keeled wide lemmas and extremely short awns.
field_matrix.quick_rule: Large flat boat-shaped spikelet + absent or tiny awns → rescuegrass candidate; preserve photo specimen until verified.

not_reliable_alone: Whole seedhead DROOP or its green/tan color
One unmeasured spikelet or awn when close annual species overlap
Hairy leaf sheath alone (several bromes have hairs)
YELLOW anthers: a widespread grass flowering character
Dry shriveled base mistaken for annual/perennial crown
Any native county claim derived from a state native designation rather than voucher evidence

field_id_finish_pass.crew_teaching_summary: Native North American woodland PERENNIAL with a fairly tall loose, drooping flowering head, relatively broad soft leaves, and hairy sheaths. Check a true membranous ligule and awned multi-flowered spikelets. This existing photograph is low resolution, so lemma-level confirmation remains OPEN.
field_id_finish_pass.lookalike_comparison: Unlike the three other currently installed Bromus cards, B. pubescens is PERENNIAL and often found in shaded moist woodland understory. Japanese brome is a small-spikeleted annual with flexuous panicle branches; B. lanceolatus has unusually long, many-flowered annual spikelets; B. texensis is an annual with shorter awns and requires mature glume/lemma comparison. Habitat or hairiness alone cannot clinch this one.

field_photo_quickcheck.heading: Hairy woodland brome — measure ONE spikelet, then compare the other bromes
steps: Look at the verified, source-attributed original photo: identify PANICLE branches, a single MULTIFLOWERED spikelet and the bristle attached to a LEMMA if visible.
Check ROOTED plant duration. Only B. pubescens is a persistent perennial among the FOUR installed bromes; rescuegrass can vary annual to short-lived perennial.
Put a 1-mm ruler beside a ripe full spikelet. Count florets and measure TOTAL spikelet, one lower and upper glume, one fertile lemma and the AWN attached to that lemma.
Compare against the five-way key. Rescuegrass is a COMPARISON-ONLY plant: LARGE FLAT keeled spikelets and essentially no long awns.
Where Japanese vs native Texas brome (or any intermediate) remains uncertain, preserve Bromus sp. and seek lower/upper GLUME VENATION macro before a management decision.
field_photo_quickcheck.field_rule: Brome genus = many florets per spikelet in a branching panicle; species depends on whole plant duration, spikelet compression, verified glume-vein/lemma/awn dimensions—not just color or droop.
field_photo_quickcheck.warning: Original source photo arrows only depict gross visible structures. No installed photo proves tiny vein counts or measured mature lemma teeth. Do not label B. catharticus installed or claim a new Hays County native status.

what_to_photograph_for_confirmation: Same-plant whole flowering panicle plus rooted annual/perennial crown, 1-cm ruler.
One mature complete spikelet from several branches at 1-mm scale with individual florets counted.
Separate lower/upper GLUMES backlit showing actual nerve count and measurable endpoints.
Mature lemma body and AWN in one focus plane, awn attached just below/to apex, and any two tip teeth.
True leaf blade–sheath collar, membranous ligule and sheath hairs on the same photographed culm.
For rescuegrass comparison, SHOW spikelet from face and side to confirm strong flattening and a really SHORT/absent awn.
